## StandardDrawing.kt { #standarddrawing-kt }

The small vocabulary of `FLine` construction and styling that sketches and examples reach for
first.

`fline` is the builder; the `rangeTo` operator makes a one-segment line out of two vectors
(`a..b`, composable with `+=`), and the styling overloads of `moveTo` / `lineTo` / `cubicTo`
position a node and style it in the same call. Appearance is carried by delegated properties on
`FLine` and `FLine.Node` — `color`, `thickness`, `thicken`, `filled`, `stroked`, `pointed`,
`pointSize` — which the renderers read back; `onClick` and `hoverColor` only do anything in the
interactive outputs.

The rest are shape helpers: `rect` and `Rect.toFLine`, `arrow` (a real filled arrowhead rather
than a point sprite), `seg`, and `fitInto`, which scales and centres a list of lines into a
`Rect` using their 2D bounds only.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/StandardDrawing.kt`

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [Neighbors & graph connectivity to FLine examples](../graph_connectivity_examples.md), [Boolean networks to FLine examples](../boolean_networks_examples.md)

## ArchitecturalGeometry.kt { #architecturalgeometry-kt }

A named, typed DSL over the raw constraint vocabulary in `CeresGeometry.kt`, plus the interactive
machinery for solving it while a user drags. `geometryModel` opens a [`GeometryModelScope`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-geometrymodelscope) where
you declare [`PointRef`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-pointref)s, [`LineRef`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-lineref)s, [`PlaneRef`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-planeref)s and [`PanelRef`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-panelref)s (points can be created from
`Vector3fc` values or bound to live `Vector3f`s via `GeometryModelScope.bindPoint`) and then
state relations inside `constraints { }` — [`ConstraintScope`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-constraintscope) supplies `length`, `parallelTo`,
`angleRadiansTo`, `planar`, `on`, `inside`, `lock`, `weak`, `mirror`, `dihedral` and the `ceq`
infix equality.

`GeometryModel.openSession` (or `session`) compiles the program once and returns a
[`GeometrySolveSession`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-geometrysolvesession) holding a mutable point cloud, per-point prior weights and a reusable
solve report; `GeometrySolveSession.drag` / [`DragHandle`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-draghandle) / `pin` / `release` are the interaction
verbs, weighted by [`InteractionPolicy`](graphics.md#interactivesolving-kt-interactionpolicy).

`liveGeometry` wraps a model *block* rather than a model: each `LiveGeometryProgram.step` re-runs
the block, reuses the existing session when point names, point count and program hash are all
unchanged, reads every bound point back in, solves, and writes the results out through the
bindings. `LiveGeometryProgram.polishLocked` does a separate hard-locked settle pass.

Point arithmetic ([`PointExpr`](graphics.md#architecturalgeometry-kt-pointexpr), `a + b`, `0.5 * c`) creates synthetic "trace" points that are
recomputed from their expression before every solve. The default backend is `FfmCeresBackend`, so
these entry points need the native Ceres library present.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/ceres/ArchitecturalGeometry.kt`

## CeresGeometry.kt { #ceresgeometry-kt }

The constraint vocabulary for Field's Ceres point solver, and the encoding that ships it to a
backend. Geometry is a flat xyz [`PointCloud`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-pointcloud) addressed by [`PointId`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-pointid); a solve is described by a
[`CeresProgram`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresprogram) of [`GeometryConstraint`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-geometryconstraint)s — [`Planar`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-planar), [`Colinear`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-colinear), [`DistanceEquals`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-distanceequals),
[`Perpendicular`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-perpendicular), [`LockPosition`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-lockposition), [`WeakPosition`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-weakposition), [`PointOnPlane`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-pointonplane), [`DihedralAngle`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-dihedralangle), [`PanelArea`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-panelarea) and
the rest — most conveniently assembled with `buildCeresProgram` / [`CeresProgramBuilder`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresprogrambuilder).

Every constraint serialises itself into one flat `DoubleArray` of opcodes ([`CeresOpcode`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresopcode)) via
`encodeLegacyBytecode`, and declares the [`CeresFeature`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceresfeature) a backend must support to run it; the
actual solving happens behind [`CeresSolverBackend`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-ceressolverbackend) / [`CompiledCeresSolver`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-compiledceressolver) (see
`FfmCeresBackend.kt` for the native one). [`CachedCeresSolvers`](graphics.md#ceresgeometry-kt-cachedceressolvers) keys compiled solvers by point
count plus program hash so an unchanged program is compiled once.

Constructors validate aggressively: coordinates and weights must be finite, weights non-negative,
point indices distinct where the opcode requires it, and the `-1`/`PointId.ALL_POINTS` sentinel
may only be used alone and only where a constraint allows it.

## InteractiveSolving.kt { #interactivesolving-kt }

The mutable, reuse-oriented half of the Ceres solver API, for solving the same program over and
over at interactive rates. [`MutablePointCloud`](graphics.md#interactivesolving-kt-mutablepointcloud), [`MutablePriorWeights`](graphics.md#interactivesolving-kt-mutablepriorweights) and [`MutableSolveReport`](graphics.md#interactivesolving-kt-mutablesolvereport)
are in-place counterparts to the immutable `PointCloud` / `DynamicPriorWeights` / `SolveMetrics`
in `CeresGeometry.kt`, so a drag loop can call `ReusableCompiledCeresSolver.solveInPlace` without
allocating a new point cloud or result per frame.

[`InteractionPolicy`](graphics.md#interactivesolving-kt-interactionpolicy) collects the weights and iteration counts that distinguish the three phases
of a drag — a cheap `dragOptions` pass while the mouse is down, a longer `releaseOptions` settle
on release, and `pinnedWeight` for points held fixed — and precomputes the matching
`SolveOptions`.
`MutableSolveReport.top` names the highest-cost opcode groups from the last solve.

All point and weight arrays are flat xyz triples; coordinates must be finite and weights finite
and non-negative, and a report's group capacity must be at least the metric capacity a solve
asks for.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/ceres/InteractiveSolving.kt`

## colors.kt { #colors-kt }

Colour constructors for the stdlib. Everything here returns a `Vec4` of sRGB-encoded components
clamped to `[0,1]` with alpha last, so the results drop straight into FLine colours and uniforms.

`rgb` / `rgba` accept either 0..1 or 0..255 components — the scale is inferred per call from
whether any component exceeds 1 — and `rgb255` forces the 0..255 reading. `hsl` is ordinary HSL;
`okhsl` and `okhsv` are the Oklab-based equivalents, which hold perceived lightness far steadier
across hue. Hue may be given as a fraction of a turn or in degrees (magnitude above 1 is divided
by 360) and is wrapped either way.

For sets: `hueSetHsl`, `hueSetOkhsl` and `hueSetOkhsv` (aliased `hslSet`, `okhslSet`, `okhsvSet`)
space equally-separated hues around the wheel at a fixed saturation and lightness.
`paletteForBackground` starts from the same okhsl ring but then walks each entry's lightness up
or down until it clears a minimum WCAG contrast ratio against the supplied background, returning
the highest-contrast candidate it found when it cannot reach the target.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/colors.kt`

**Used in:** [Colors to FLine examples](../colors_examples.md)

## contours.kt { #contours-kt }

Marching-squares iso-contours for 2D scalar fields, plus the scalar field most callers want to
contour.

A field is just a [`ScalarField2D`](graphics.md#contours-kt-scalarfield2d), `(Double, Double) -> Double`. `pointEdgeScalarField2D` builds
one from points and edges — or from a 2D `FLine` — as the union of weighted discs and capsules,
signed so that `iso = 0.0` is the tube boundary; it re-reads the supplied point list on every
sample, so mutating those `Vec2`s moves the field live. `generateIsoContours` samples a field on
an `nx` by `ny` grid and returns stitched polylines, `generateIsoContoursWithStep` takes a target
cell size instead, and the `FLine` overloads choose the sampling window from the line's 2D bounds
grown by the tube radius.

`smoothIsoContours` and `generateSmoothIsoContours` fit cubic splines through the polylines,
treating a contour that ends on the sampling bounds as open and the rest as closed loops. Two
known roughnesses: the four-crossing saddle cell is split arbitrarily, and the segment stitcher
is O(m^2) in the number of segments, so very high grid resolutions get expensive.

## fline_graph_connectivity.kt { #fline-graph-connectivity-kt }

Bridge from drawn geometry to the graph algorithms: turns one or more `FLine`s into a welded
point graph.

`flineGraph`, or the `toFLineGraph` extensions on `FLine` and `Iterable<FLine>`, adaptively
subdivides cubics down to `cubicFlatness`, samples every node, then welds samples closer than
`epsilon` using a uniform grid plus union-find (`epsilon = 0` welds only bit-identical
positions). A welded vertex is the mean of the samples that reached it, and
`FLineGraph.vertexSources` records which line index and node instruction each of those samples
came from. Edges join consecutive samples, `close()` joins back to the subpath start,
self-edges are dropped and duplicates collapse to the shortest.

The result carries a `PointGraph` of `GraphEdge`s — the same types as `graph_connectivity.kt` —
so the search, spanning-tree and analysis functions there apply directly to a drawing.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/fline_graph_connectivity.kt`

## graph_connectivity.kt { #graph-connectivity-kt }

Self-contained graph / computational-geometry library over 2D and 3D point sets
(`Vec2`/`Vec3`). Every algorithm has a `vec2*` and (where meaningful) a `vec3*` entry point
returning a [`PointGraph`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-pointgraph); see each function's own KDoc for its definition and complexity.

Proximity / neighbourhood families: KNN (`vec2KnnGraph`), Orthant (`vec2OrthantGraph`),
Relative Neighborhood (`vec2RelativeNeighborhoodGraph`), Gabriel (`vec2GabrielGraph`),
Beta-Skeleton (`vec2BetaSkeleton`), Nearest-Neighbor (`vec2NearestNeighborGraph`),
Minimum Spanning Tree (`vec2MinimumSpanningTree`), Maximum-Diameter/radius
(`vec2MaximumDiameterGraph`), Maximum-Cut (`vec2MaximumCutGraph`) and Complete
(`vec2CompleteGraph`) graphs.

JTS-backed (2D only): full Delaunay triangulation (`vec2DelaunayGraph`, `vec2DelaunayTriangles`),
Urquhart (`vec2UrquhartGraph`, a real Urquhart graph built by removing the longest edge of each
Delaunay triangle — the 3D `vec3UrquhartGraph` is an MST approximation because Field only wires
2D Delaunay), Voronoi diagram/dual (`vec2VoronoiDiagram`, `vec2VoronoiDualGraph`) and convex
hull (`vec2ConvexHull`, `vec2ConvexHullGraph`, `vec2HullProjectionGraph`).

Traversal / analysis: BFS/DFS/A* path search, [`GraphEdgeVisitState`](graphics.md#graph-connectivity-kt-graphedgevisitstate) greedy walks and
graph-diameter path decomposition (see the search/path functions below), plus FLine rendering
integration in `fline_graph_connectivity.kt`.

Custom distance metrics: pass `GraphConnectivityOptions.customDistanceMetric`. It is honoured by
the distance-driven algorithms (KNN, MST, RNG, Gabriel, Beta-Skeleton, Delaunay/Urquhart edge
weights, etc.). This includes `vec2OrthantGraph`/`vec3OrthantGraph`, whose nearest-neighbour
ranking within each orthant honours `customDistanceMetric` when supplied (Euclidean otherwise).

Smoke tests: `afield.examples.stdlib.GraphConnectivitySmokeTest` (its `runTests()` drives 35
checks, covering path search, edge-visit-state and FLine rendering as well as the core graphs).
Live rendered examples: `public/docs/graph_connectivity_examples.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/graph_connectivity.kt`

**Used in:** [Neighbors & graph connectivity to FLine examples](../graph_connectivity_examples.md)

## keyframer.kt { #keyframer-kt }

Snapshot, interpolate and persist the live state of a running sketch. A [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) is a set
of named targets — uniform `Structure` bindings, the uniform structures of a `ModulePointer` /
`ComputeModulePointer` / `MeshModulePointer`, a stackAuto shader-source slot via
`KeyframeScope.stackAuto`, or a `Camera` pose via `KeyframeScope.camera`. `capture()` reads them
all into a `KeyframeScope.Key`; invoking that `Key` writes them all back.

`KeyframeScope.interpolate` blends two keys per value type: numbers and vectors lerp, quaternions
slerp, dual quaternions and `CameraPose` sclerp, and strings / [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) /
`SourceBackedBlock` step to the right-hand value at `t >= 1`. `remap` can re-time an individual
key's `t`.

Persistence goes through the [`KValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-kvalue) serial union, so only the types `KValue.fromAny` recognises
survive a save — numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL
source and source-backed block; anything else is silently dropped. Every `saveKey` also writes a
numbered copy into a `<file>.versions` directory with a manifest, which
`KeyframeScope.keyVersions` lists and `KeyframeScope.loadLatestKey` follows. `KeyframeScope.missingKey` supplies defaults for
keys absent from an older file, optionally per schema version.

Keys render themselves as HTML for box output ([`KeyDiff`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydiff), `diffHtml`), and
`copyUpdateCodeToClipboard` emits pasteable Kotlin — that one goes through the AWT clipboard.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/keyframer.kt`

**Used in:** [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md)

### NumKind { #keyframer-kt-numkind }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NumKind</span></code>

Which Kotlin numeric type a saved number came from, so that `KValue.toAny` can hand back a `Byte`/`Short`/`Int`/`Long`/`Float`/`Double` rather than always a `Double` — a uniform bound to an `Int` has to come back as an `Int`.

Constants: `BYTE`, `SHORT`, `INT`, `LONG`, `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`.

### KValue { #keyframer-kt-kvalue }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code>

The closed set of value types a `KeyframeScope.Key` can *persist*: numbers, vec2/3/4, quaternion, dual quaternion, camera pose, string, StackSL source and source-backed block. A key in memory holds plain Kotlin values; this is the serial union they are converted to on the way to disk and back.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Num</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NumKind</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | Any Kotlin number, kept as a `Double` with the [`NumKind`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-numkind) needed to restore its original type. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Vec2</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `Vector2f`, component by component. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Vec3</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `Vector3f`, component by component. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Vec4</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">w</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `Vector4f`, component by component — the usual RGBA or homogeneous-point uniform. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Quat</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">z</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">w</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `Quaternionf` as raw `x, y, z, w`; stored as-is, and not re-normalised on load. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">DualQuat</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realZ</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realW</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualZ</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualW</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `DualQuaternionf` — a rigid transform (rotation plus translation) as its real and dual quaternion halves. Unlike [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) this *is* normalised on the way back in, so a slightly drifted saved value is repaired on load. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">CameraPoseValue</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realZ</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">realW</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualZ</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dualW</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">focusDistance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `CameraPose`: the camera's rigid transform as a dual quaternion, plus the focus distance that says how far in front of it the thing it is looking at sits. Also normalised on load. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StackSL</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | StackSL source text, tagged as code rather than as a string so that it reloads as a [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) and interpolation steps it discretely instead of trying to blend it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Str</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A plain `String`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">SourceBlock</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">boxId</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">source</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span></code> | A `SourceBackedBlock` reduced to the box it came from and its Kotlin source — the *live lambda* is not persisted. On load the block re-compiles its source in that box on first invocation, so a key restored into a document where the box is gone throws when the value is finally called. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toAny</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span></code> | Rebuild the live Kotlin value this entry stands for — the load half of the round trip. Quaternion-shaped values are re-normalised on the way out, numbers regain their [`NumKind`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-numkind) type, and a `SourceBlock` becomes a `SourceBackedBlock` that has not compiled anything yet. |

class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

What a saved key looks like on disk: a schema version and a name → [`KValue`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-kvalue) map, pretty-printed as JSON with `type` as the discriminator.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | The owning scope's `schemaVersion` at the moment of saving. Nothing validates it on load: a mismatch is not an error, it only selects which `KeyframeScope.missingKey` defaults apply. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">KValue</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | The key's entries by name. Values that `KValue.fromAny` could not represent are already gone. |

One row of a key file's version history, as recorded in the `<file>.versions/manifest.json` that every `saveKey` appends to. `KeyframeScope.keyVersions` hands these back, sorted by `index`.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Monotonic version number, starting at 0 and simply "highest so far plus one" — a save counter, not a schema version and not related to `KeyDTO.schemaVersion`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timestamp</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | When the version was written, as an ISO-8601 `Instant.now()` string in UTC. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">note</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Whatever note was passed to `saveKey`, for telling two snapshots apart later. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">file</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | File name inside the `.versions` directory, `"%06d.json"` of `index`. |

### StackSLString { #keyframer-kt-stackslstring }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">StackSLString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A string that a [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) should treat as *code* rather than as text: StackSL source.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">toString</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The StackSL source itself, so a `StackSLString` prints and concatenates like the string it wraps. |

### KeyframeScope { #keyframer-kt-keyframescope }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">KeyframeScope</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">schemaVersion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>

A named set of live things worth snapshotting — uniform `Structure` bindings, a module's live uniforms, a `stack.auto` shader slot, a `Camera` — plus the machinery to capture, blend, save and reload them. This is the object you keep around for the lifetime of a sketch.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">targets</span></code> | The statically-bound targets, by key name, as registered by `target(name, structure)` — exposed so you can see and clear what a scope is watching. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">remap</span></code> | Per-key re-timing for `interpolate`: `remap["gain"] = { t -> t * t * (3 - 2 * t) }` eases that one value on a smoothstep while everything else stays linear. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">inner</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Key</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ToHTML</span></code> | One snapshot: names to values, and the ability to put them all back. Get one from `capture`, `interpolate`, `loadKey`, or by constructing it from a map you wrote by hand (as the docs examples do). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">structure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Structure</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a key `name` against a uniform `structure` held for good — the simplest target, for a `Structure` you built once and will keep. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">structure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Structure</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a key `name` against a structure that is looked up **again on every read and write** — the right choice for anything a shader reload can replace underneath you. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a key against one of a graphics module's live uniform structures, resolved through the pointer each time so it survives a shader reload. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ComputeModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `target` for a compute module's live uniform structures. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">target</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MeshModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `target` for a mesh-shader module's live uniform structures. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">stackAuto</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">keyName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a key against a `stack.auto.<name>` **shader-source** slot, so that the StackSL a module runs is part of the snapshot: capture reads it as a [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring) and applying a key recompiles the slot. This is what lets a keyframe morph a patch's code as well as its numbers. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">stackAuto</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ComputeModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">keyName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `stackAuto` for a compute module; the source is reloaded on the compute path. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">stackAuto</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">module</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MeshModulePointer</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">keyName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">name</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | `stackAuto` for a mesh-shader module; the source is reloaded on the mesh path. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">camera</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">camera</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Camera</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">keyName</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="s">&quot;camera&quot;</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Register a `Camera` as a keyable target, so a viewpoint can be snapshotted and morphed like any other value. Capture stores the camera's `CameraPose` — its rigid transform plus focus distance — and applying a key calls `applyPose`, so `interpolate` gives you a screw-motion (sclerp) camera move rather than a separate position and target lerp. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">findByName</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">name</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">Function0</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="o">&#42;</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Unit</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The raw "bind a lambda to this target" function for a registered key `name`, or null if there is no such key — an escape hatch for driving a target continuously instead of through a `Key`. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">capture</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code> | Read every registered target *right now* into a new `Key` — the snapshot call. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">interpolate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">a</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Key</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">b</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Key</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">t</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Key</span></code> | Blend two snapshots into a new `Key` at position `t`, per value type: numbers and vectors lerp, quaternions slerp, dual quaternions and camera poses sclerp, and strings, [`StackSLString`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-stackslstring)s and source blocks **step** to `b`'s value once `t >= 1` — code never gets a half-parsed intermediate. |

### KeyDiffKind { #keyframer-kt-keydiffkind }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">KeyDiffKind</span></code>

How one name differs between two keys, always read left-to-right: `ADDED` means the right key has it and the left does not, `REMOVED` the other way round, `CHANGED` that both have it with unequal values. There is no "same" kind — unchanged names are left out of a diff entirely.

Constants: `ADDED`, `REMOVED`, `CHANGED`.

## modelling.kt { #modelling-kt }

A self-tuning controller for pushing the *distribution* of a scalar signal towards a target
shape. You hand `AdaptiveDistributionController.pushSamples` a batch of samples each frame and it
returns a [`ControlOutput`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controloutput) whose `appliedParams` are the next parameter values to send to whatever
produced them — a shader, a simulation, a tone curve.

The error signal comes from a [`FeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-featureextractor); [`UniformQuantileFeatureExtractor`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-uniformquantilefeatureextractor) is the
built-in one and measures how far a set of sample quantiles sit from their targets. Internally
each feature gets a recursive-least-squares row (with forgetting) that learns a local Jacobian,
the step is a Tikhonov-regularised Gauss-Newton solve scaled by a confidence estimate, then
softened near the parameter bounds, rate-limited by `maxStep`, clipped, and finally offset by a
per-parameter sinusoidal dither so the estimator keeps seeing excitation.

`ControllerConfig.observationDelayFrames` is the important knob: it models pipeline latency
explicitly by pairing each observation with the command issued that many pushes earlier, so the
loop does not have to be slowed down to learn correctly. Use [`AdaptiveDistributionControllerBank`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributioncontrollerbank)
for one controller per scene, and [`AdaptiveDistributionLoop`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-adaptivedistributionloop) to drive `observe`/`apply` from a
`Runloop` hook.

This is plain `DoubleArray` math with no GPU or `Box` dependency; every array in
[`ControllerConfig`](graphics.md#modelling-kt-controllerconfig) must be `parameterNames.size` long. `main` runs a synthetic drifting-Gaussian
plant against the controller and prints a trace.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/modelling.kt`

## quantilewarp.kt { #quantilewarp-kt }

Reshapes a scalar signal's distribution by fitting a monotone 8-knot PCHIP curve from the
measured quantiles of recent samples onto the quantiles of a chosen target distribution —
`TargetDistributions.UnitNormal` by default, or any [`QuantileFunction`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilefunction).

`AdaptiveQuantileWarp.update` takes a batch of samples, merges it with the last
`historyFrames` batches, and returns a [`QuantileWarpState`](graphics.md#quantilewarp-kt-quantilewarpstate): the knot pairs, an
`QuantileWarpState.evaluate` for CPU-side use, and the same 16 knots packed into four `vec4`s
ready for push constants via `QuantileWarpState.applyToPushConstants`. Successive states are
smoothed towards each other by `smoothingAlpha` and forced strictly increasing, so the curve
stays invertible even when the input degenerates.

`fieldQuantileWarpIncludeSource` is the matching GLSL — `fieldQuantileWarp8` and
`fieldQuantileWarpMix` evaluate the identical PCHIP curve on the GPU — and is reachable from
shader source as the built-in include named by `FIELD_QUANTILE_WARP_INCLUDE_NAME`.
`Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` closes the loop: it installs a runloop hook that drains a
`ShaderFieldProbe`, updates the warp, calls your `apply` callback and renders a knot table into a
box display channel.

Constraints worth knowing: exactly eight strictly increasing probabilities inside `(0, 1)`, and
the `Box.fieldProbeQuantileWarp` entry point needs a live `Box` plus a probe configured for
continuous snapshot reads.

## shaders.kt { #shaders-kt }

The bridge between a box's text and a live Vulkan pipeline: shader source lives in box
properties, and this file turns it into modules and keeps them hot-reloading.

The properties come first — `vertex`, `fragment`, `compute`, `task`/`mesh`, the ray-tracing
stages, and a `_s` variant of each for Slang — alongside `once.vertex { }`-style seeders. The
user-facing entry points are the macro placeholders `Box.moduleHere`, `Box.computeModuleHere`,
`Box.meshModuleHere`, `Box.rayTracingModuleHere` and `Box.shadertoyHere`; each one throws
`MacroNotExpandedException` if actually called, because `MacroRegistry` is expected to rewrite it
into the real `_moduleHere`-family call.

Before compilation every stage goes through `preprocess`, which resolves `#include`s against
other boxes' shader properties (with cycle detection and `#line` fixups), against built-in
includes such as the field probe, field stats and quantile warp, and against registered include
roots — `registerShaderFilesystemIncludeRoot` for a directory and `registerLygiaIncludeRoot` /
`shaderCachedUrlIncludeRootResolver` for URL-fetched, disk-cached libraries. It also expands
`{% copyPC %}` (copying a previous stage's push-constant block) and stackAuto template slots
compiled from StackSL via `stackAutoShaderSource`.

`reloadShader`, `reloadComputeShader`, `reloadMeshShader` and `reloadRayTracingShader` are the
reload path: compile, report errors back onto the box's source lines, introspect the result, and
rewrite the box's Kotlin preamble with generated binding structures before swapping the module.
`Box.attachShader` adopts an externally built module into that same path. `Box.fieldProbeHere`,
`Box.fieldStatsHere` and `Box.fieldProbeAutoControl` attach the GPU readback instrumentation.

Everything here needs a live `Box` — properties, error reporting, preamble edits and the
generation-guarded async reload all key off it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/shaders.kt`

**Used in:** [How Box Code Runs](../box_code_pipeline.md), [afield.four Graphics](../afield_four_graphics.md), [Field Probes — instrumenting shaders](../field_probes.md)

### Top-level values { #shaders-kt-values }

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">fragment</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The fragment-stage GLSL for this box, as text — the shader tab you type into, and the *only* place a graphics module's fragment shader comes from (assignments inside a `moduleHere { }` lambda do not set it). |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">vertex</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The vertex-stage GLSL for this box. Its `layout(location = …) in` declarations are the contract that generates the box's `Mesh` writers (`pos`, `col`, …), so changing an input here changes the Kotlin API of every box downstream of the next reload. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">vertex&#95;fragment</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | One Slang source holding *both* the vertex and fragment stages, compiled twice (once per stage) by `slangc`. It beats `vertex`, `fragment`, `vertex_s` and `fragment_s` outright: when this is non-blank it is the source for both graphics stages. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">task</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The task-shader (amplification) stage GLSL of a mesh-shader pipeline. `meshModuleHere` needs `task`, `mesh` *and* `fragment` — there is no task-less mesh path here — and seeds a small `EmitMeshTasksEXT` default into all three if the box has none. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">mesh</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The mesh-shader stage GLSL, the stage that emits vertices and primitives directly (`SetMeshOutputsEXT` / `gl_MeshVerticesEXT`) instead of consuming a vertex buffer. Paired with `Box.task` and `Box.fragment` by `meshModuleHere`; note the name collides conceptually with `Mesh` the Kotlin draw object, which is unrelated. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">fragment&#95;s</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Slang source for the fragment stage. When non-blank it wins over `Box.fragment` and is transpiled to GLSL by `slangc` before shaderc ever sees it, so compile errors arrive in Slang's `(line): error` format — which `numberFromErrorMessage` does understand. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">vertex&#95;s</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Slang source for the vertex stage; wins over `Box.vertex` when non-blank. Prefer `Box.vertex_fragment` if you want the two stages to share declarations — two separate `_s` properties are transpiled independently and cannot see each other. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">task&#95;s</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Slang source for the task stage; wins over `Box.task` when non-blank. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">mesh&#95;s</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Slang source for the mesh stage; wins over `Box.mesh` when non-blank. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="nc">Box</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">&#95;fragment</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The *prepared* fragment GLSL: box-local, post-`#include`-template, post-`{% copyPC %}`, post-Slang-transpile — literally the text handed to shaderc. Written by every prepare pass and read by `_moduleHere`, which throws a `NullPointerException` if no pass ever ran. |

One `#include` that landed inside a registered include root, handed to a [`ShaderIncludeRootResolver`](graphics.md#shaders-kt-shaderincluderootresolver) to turn into text.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">root</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The registered root name that matched — the first path segment of a `root/…` include, or, for a relative include, the root the *including* file itself came from. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">includePath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | The path within `root`, normalised: separators unified to `/`, `.` and empty segments dropped, `..` resolved (and rejected if it would escape the root), no leading slash. This is the key a resolver should look up. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">requestedPath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Exactly what the `#include` said, root prefix and all. Useful in diagnostics; do not resolve against it. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">requestingSourcePath</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The resolved path of the file doing the including (a previous resolution's `resolvedPath`, or a `field/<box>-<id>/<property>.glsl` name for box source), or `null` when shaderc did not supply one. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">includeType</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderIncludeType</span></code> | `RELATIVE` for `#include "…"`, `STANDARD` for `#include <…>`. Only `RELATIVE` includes are resolved relative to `requestingSourcePath`'s directory. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">includeDepth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span></code> | How deep this include is nested, straight from shaderc. Informational — nothing in Field enforces a limit on it. |

### ShaderIncludeRootResolver { #shaders-kt-shaderincluderootresolver }

<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">ShaderIncludeRootResolver</span></code>

Turns an include inside one registered root into source text. Register one under a name with `registerShaderIncludeRoot` and every `#include "thatName/whatever.glsl"` in every box's shaders goes through it.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">resolve</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderIncludeRootRequest</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderIncludeResolution</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Resolve one include, or return `null` if this root does not have it (which the caller turns into a hard error). |

Where a URL-backed include root keeps its on-disk copies, and how patient it is with the network.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">cacheDirectory</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Path</span></code> | Directory the fetched includes are mirrored into, one file per include path. Created on demand. Resolved to an absolute, normalised path, and includes that would escape it are rejected — a remote server cannot talk you into writing outside this directory. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">connectTimeoutMillis</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | `HttpURLConnection` connect timeout, in milliseconds. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">readTimeoutMillis</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | `HttpURLConnection` read timeout, in milliseconds. Both timeouts are felt by whichever thread is compiling — the main runloop, on the reload path — so the defaults are deliberately short. |

How `Box.fieldProbeAutoControl` turns probe read-backs into controller updates: when a batch is big enough to act on, what counts as clipped, and where the diagnostics card goes.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">minSamples</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | Minimum samples in a read-back before the controller is allowed to learn from it. A snapshot with fewer is skipped entirely — `tick()` returns `null` and nothing is applied. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clipLower</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Values at or below this (within `clipEpsilon`) count as clipped low and are reported to the controller as a clip rate; `null` means "nothing clips at the bottom". |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clipUpper</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Values at or above this (within `clipEpsilon`) count as clipped high; `null` means nothing clips at the top. With both bounds `null` the reported clip rate is a flat `0.0`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clipEpsilon</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Tolerance for the two clip comparisons — floating-point slop, not a percentage. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">useNominalParams</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | `true` applies the controller's *nominal* parameters, `false` (the default) its *applied* ones, which carry the small dither the controller needs to identify the system. Turn it on once identification has settled and the dither is visible in the output. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">displayChannel</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Box output channel for the HTML diagnostics table (nominal vs applied parameters, objective, confidence, clip rate, p10/p50/p90). `null` disables the display entirely, which is what a headless test wants. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">closeDisplayOnStop</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Whether `stop()` closes the display channel by default. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clearDisplayOnStop</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code> | Whether `stop()` clears the display channel's contents by default. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">runloopKeySuffix</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span></code> | Prefix of the runloop hook key, which is `"$runloopKeySuffix:${box.id}"`. Two controllers on one box need two different values here or the second silently displaces the first. |

The running loop that closes a shader's feedback circuit: read the probe, push the samples into an adaptive controller, hand the new parameters to your `apply` lambda, and draw the diagnostics.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">box</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Box</span></code> | The box this controller belongs to: the source of the display channel and the identity in the runloop hook key. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">probe</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderFieldProbe</span></code> | The probe being read. `Box.fieldProbeAutoControl` has already put it into continuous-read mode, so it delivers a snapshot every frame rather than at the display rate. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">controller</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AdaptiveDistributionController</span></code> | The adaptive controller doing the actual learning; its `parameterNames` label the diagnostics table and its `pushSamples` is what turns a batch into parameters. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">config</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderProbeAutoControlConfig</span></code> | The thresholds, clip bounds and display settings this controller was built with. Read on every tick, but the object is immutable — copy it and rebuild to change your mind. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">tickCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many ticks have actually done work. Ticks that found no new snapshot, or too few samples, do not count — so a `tickCount` stuck at zero means the probe is not delivering, not that the hook is missing. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">lastBatch</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">FieldProbeScalarBatch</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The last probe batch the controller learned from, or `null` before the first useful tick. Carries both the raw snapshot and the clip rate computed from `config`. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">lastOutput</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ControlOutput</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | The last controller output — nominal and applied parameters plus diagnostics — or `null` before the first useful tick. The same object the `apply` lambda was handed. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">tick</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ControlOutput</span><span class="o">?</span></code> | Do one control step, returning the controller's output, or `null` if there was nothing to do. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">install</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">runloop</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Runloop</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Runloop</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">runLoop</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderFieldAutoController</span></code> | Install a `preRun` hook that calls `tick` once per frame, and return `this` for chaining. Idempotent — a second call while already installed does nothing. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">stop</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">runloop</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Runloop</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Runloop</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">runLoop</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">closeDisplay</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">config</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">closeDisplayOnStop</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">clearDisplay</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">config</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">clearDisplayOnStop</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ShaderFieldAutoController</span></code> | Remove the runloop hook, optionally tidy the display channel, and forget this controller on the box. Returns `this`, and can be re-`install`ed afterwards. |

## stacksl.kt { #stacksl-kt }

Host-side entry points for StackSL: compiling the stack language to GLSL, and evaluating it on
the GPU sample by sample. The language, its compiler and its diagnostics live in
`afield.stacksl`; this file is the Kotlin surface a box calls.

`stackSL` holds a box's StackSL source, falling back to a parent box's. `compileStackSL`,
`stackSLToGlsl` and the standalone `slGlsl` are pure compilation and need no device. `slEval` and
`slSweep` actually run the compiled function: they wrap it in a small compute shader and dispatch
it through a `Renderer` that defaults to `fromContext()`, so they need a live graphics context.
Neither binds any texture sampler, so a source that needs one is rejected.

`slSweep` returns a [`StackSLSweep`](graphics.md#stacksl-kt-stackslsweep), which implements `ToHTML` and draws itself as an inline SVG
plot of the four output channels with per-channel min/median/max; `StackSLSweep.h` is that HTML.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/stdlib/stacksl.kt`

**Used in:** [StackSL cheatsheet](../stacksl_cheatsheet.md), [StackSL examples](../stacksl_examples.md)

What `slSweep` measured: the inputs it used and the `vec4` the program returned for each, kept side by side so the response can be plotted or asserted on.

May contain NaN or infinity. |
| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">size</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code> | How many samples the sweep holds — the `samples` `slSweep` was asked for. |

| <code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">channel</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">channel</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Float</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | One output channel across the whole sweep, as a list ready for a plot: `0` is x/r, `1` y/g, `2` z/b, `3` w/a. Any other index throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Non-finite samples are handed back as they are — it is the plot, not this, that filters them. |

## voronoi.kt { #voronoi-kt }

Practical 3D Voronoi and approximate 3D multiplicatively weighted Voronoi
("CircularDirichlet") for Kotlin + Field linalg.

- voronoi3d(...) builds convex polyhedral cells by intersecting pairwise
  bisector half-spaces, then closing unbounded cells against a large clip box.
- CircularDirichlet3d.build(...) extracts approximate support patches on
  bisector spheres / planes by clipping a sampled surface mesh with the
  weighted score predicate.

The weighted contourer is renderer-oriented: it prefers stable, wound
boundary loops over exact symbolic patch topology.
